entry.title: Back to 3D Printing: From Anycubic 4MAX to Ender 3 Pro
entry.summary: Returning to 3D printing with an Ender 3 Pro, from endless toolhead upgrades to printing useful things at home.
entry.content:
In February 2021, I wrote My first steps in 3D printing, where I talked about my first 3D printer, the Anycubic 4MAX, its upgrades, and how I eventually ended up disappointed with the results of those modifications.

Unfortunately, my Anycubic 4MAX is still gathering dust somewhere in Russia. In Belgrade, I returned to 3D printing with a Creality Ender 3 Pro—a printer I'd had my eye on for quite a while and had even considered buying as a second printer.

From OctoPrint to Klipper

Back in Russia, I bought a Raspberry Pi 3B and used it to run OctoPrint with the Anycubic 4MAX. I wanted to start prints remotely and have a web interface for it.

I brought the Raspberry Pi with me from Russia, and it came in very handy in Belgrade.

Almost immediately after buying the Ender 3 Pro, I connected the Raspberry Pi to its stock motherboard and installed Klipper.

Later, I replaced the stock motherboard with an SKR Mini E3 V3.0.

It's a kind of drop-in replacement: you can install it in place of the original board without modifying the electronics enclosure.

What I mainly wanted from the new board was quieter stepper drivers and the ability to control the hotend cooling fan, so it wouldn't have to run all the time.

Endless Toolhead Upgrades

Unlike my previous experience, I started paying more attention to ready-made solutions that could be installed with minimal modifications. But I didn't arrive at that approach straight away.

There are countless mods available for the Ender 3, and I decided to take advantage of them. At first, I tried upgrading the cooling system with the Hero Me project. Buying a Sprite Pro seemed expensive and unnecessary at the time: I could build Hero Me from printed parts and essentially repackage the existing extruder.

But I ran into problems.

That combination of hotend and filament feeder required a Bowden tube between the hotend heatsink and the feeder. And that tube caused an enormous amount of trouble later on.

I just couldn't put the toolhead together properly, and I wasn't particularly happy with the design itself. I spent a very long time tinkering with it but never managed to get a result I was satisfied with.

I decided this part of the setup needed to be simpler, and even bought a BMG extruder to replace the Ender 3 Pro's stock feeder.

But that didn't help either.

Then I thought I'd probably use the BMG together with an E3D V6 hotend. That would have required a lot more modifications, though, and by then my toolhead was already in pieces.

At some point, I decided it would be better to buy a Sprite Pro, install it, and just start printing instead of endlessly rebuilding the toolhead.

The kit included the extruder itself, a carriage compatible with the Ender 3 Pro, a cable, and the other necessary parts. That meant I could keep additional modifications to a minimum and get back to printing as soon as possible.

Sprite Pro and Finding a Stable Setup

Of course, I still couldn't give up modifications completely.

Even for the Sprite Pro, I found a way to modify the mounting plate and cooling system to use 5015 fans. The stock fans didn't seem powerful enough to me.

But this time I kept in mind that I didn't have a spare extruder, so I needed to be very careful with modifications.

That process was also somewhat painful and took quite a bit of time. Still, after several iterations, I finally arrived at a reasonably stable setup that I'm happy with.

Sprite Pro with my modified cooling setup.

A Printer as a Tool for the Home

In the end, I decided to use this printer exclusively for PLA and PETG.

What I mainly want from it is the ability to print things and parts for the home that make everyday life a little better.

As it turns out, when you can design something yourself or find a suitable model on a dedicated website, a 3D printer becomes a very handy tool.

Being able to make a small part for exactly the task you have in mind can really improve everyday life.

Volkswagen Golf — Just for Fun

One of those models is a little Volkswagen Golf.

When I found this Volkswagen Golf GTI Mk1 model on Printables, I immediately fell for it. I printed it simply because I wanted something nice to look at.

Not everything you print has to serve a practical purpose.

The little Volkswagen Golf GTI Mk1 I printed just for fun.

A Funnel for the Dishwasher

Another example is a funnel for pouring salt into the dishwasher.

The dishwasher didn't come with a funnel. Going to a shop or buying one separately seemed unnecessary.

I simply found a suitable model online and printed it quickly.

Now, every time I refill the dishwasher salt, the funnel does its job: the salt doesn't spill, and I'm happy.

A small printed funnel for refilling dishwasher salt.

Instead of a Conclusion

I used to get a huge amount of enjoyment out of upgrading the printer itself. These days, my priorities have changed a little: I'd rather use it to make things. Sometimes I still get the urge to modify something, but when that happens, I remember what my academic supervisor used to tell me: “Perfection is not when there is nothing left to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.” And although my Ender 3 Pro is already outdated in some respects, I'm quite happy with its current setup, and it covers my basic home-printing needs.

entry.title: Magic of Python packages
entry.content:
Magic of Python packages

There is always some magic when you learn python and install packages with pip install command. But have you ever wondered how python packages are born?

At first, there is almost any package for your need in the PYPI repository. PYPI is a PYthon Package Index. That is a default repository for python modules. When you install a module with pip install command, it downloads the required package and its dependencies from pypi.org. Of course that could be overwritten with your private repository instance, if you have one. 🙂 While you accumulate more and more experience with writing python code you may face some extra needs for python packages. You check pypi and voila! Wait... No. There is no package for your specific purpose. It has not been developed yet. Okay, you have an idea of how to make the package. And then you did it. Nice. It's time to share your awesome code and make other developers happy because there is no need to develop the package again. How to start?

Well, there is a great python packaging guide. I would recommend to go through it. It will help you to through the basics of packaging process. The guide includes the following steps:

  1. Preparing your package repository folder structure for packaging;
  2. Creating configuration files for packaging and distribution (license and readme);
  3. Generating distribution archives;
  4. Downloading the archives to a python index repo;
  5. And finally, installing the newly added package.

Yes, your friends will be able to install your package with pip install <your_cool_package_name> now. You may worry about making mistakes while uploading distribution archives to PYPI. Stop it 🙂 There is a test PYPI instance to master interaction with pypi repository. It is here. Don't place any valuable info there because the testing PYPI instance is periodically cleaned.

Huh. It seems that now some magic smoke disappeared and you understand more clearly of how things are done in python. Enjoy!

entry.title: Hacktoberfest2021
entry.content:
Hacktoberfest 2021 and contributing to open source

What is Hacktoberfest? It is a month-long celebration of open source software run by DigitalOcean. (More official info is available here: https://hacktoberfest.digitalocean.com/)

For me it's a time of a year to make our world better. I believe that almost every person using any products of the modern technology leverages open source. Contributing to Open Source is a modern type of charity where your donate a very valuable entity, I mean your ideas and their implementation.

That's why I like the spirit of the event and I'm very grateful to Digital Ocean for the Hacktoberfest. Also, I visited the event's official kick-off meeting and there were a lot of information for newcomers. It aimed everyone to easily start participating in open source.

entry.title: Posting to GitHub pages
entry.content:
Posting the website to Github Pages

Generating a static website was an easy task. Thanks Pelican. The output is a folder with a bunch of html and css files. All you need to make this a website is to create a public GitHub repo named your_username.github.io and push the output files into main branch there. The resulted website will be available at https://your_username.github.io. More details on GitHub Pages here: https://pages.github.com/

The first website template is a bit ugly though it is simple and understandable. So I'm gonna create my own template. It means to make blog even more uglier :D

I have an idea about how to make the blog content delivery more comfortable and faster. I will post it later.

entry.title: My first steps in 3d printing
entry.content:
My first steps in 3d printing

A couple of years ago I've bought a DIY 3d printer kit Anycubic 4MAX. I was dreaming about my own 3d printer to make cases for my electronic projects. DIY kit was a cheaper option than buying an assembled one and I also wanted to understand how things are done 'under the hood' of a 3d printer. There was a detailed instruction for the Anycubic 4max 3d printer, and I spent about 2 days putting it together. That was a real pleasure to watch the first model was printing.

Then I asked myself a question: 'What next? What things I'd like to create?' I was already familiar with sites like thingiverse.com, and it turned out that there are lots of upgrades that could be printed for my Anycubic 4max. Making upgrades for my 3d printer then became a desire. I've upgraded mother-board and extruder's coolers, printed an improved fan duct, assembled more quiet TMC2208 drivers for stepper motors. And everything was ok. My 3d printer has become quieter. I customized its settings so the print quality was great. And then I decided to install another and very hyped extruder Titan Aero. I was expecting the print quality would increase many times. I've found a model of a carriage with the Titan Aero mount for Anycubic 4max and printed it. Then I assembled it and tried to make prints. They were faulty. I had to adjust printing settings many times, do lots of calibrations, re-flash internal printer firmware to achieve the same printing quality. The extruder upgrade consumed a lot of my time, and I was very upset of my expectations haven't met the reality. Neither great quality nor speed increase appeared.

Two years have passed since then. My 3d printer was packed and gathered dust in the corner. I wanted either sell it or gift it to someone. I wanted to give up.
